chapters.title: Chapter 5: ESOPs from the Company’s Side

lessons.title: The Cost of ESOPs: Accounting Expense, Dilution and Treasury Impact

children.text: Founders often describe ESOPs as free: no cash goes out, so there is no cost. Finance teams know better, and so do investors reading the profit and loss statement. ESOPs carry three distinct costs, and only one of them involves money leaving the bank.

body.text: An ESOP costs the company an accounting expense it must report, a slice of ownership it can never take back, and, if it ever runs a buyback, real cash. Confusing these three is how boards end up surprised.

children.text: Three Costs, Three Different Places

cells: Employee benefits expense in the profit and loss statement
The cap table, and diluted earnings per share
Professional fees, valuation and platform costs

children.text: Cost One: The Accounting Expense
Under
Ind AS 102
, a company measures the
grant-date fair value

of the options, typically using Black-Scholes or a binomial model, and spreads that value as an expense across the vesting period. Note what is being valued: not the discount at exercise, but the option itself on the day it was granted.

markDefs.definition: Ind AS 102, the Indian accounting standard on share-based payment, which requires the grant-date fair value of options to be recognised as an expense over the vesting period.
The value of an option on the date it is granted, estimated with an option pricing model such as Black-Scholes, and quite different from its intrinsic value.

body.latex: \text{Annual expense} = \frac{\text{Options granted} \times \text{Grant-date fair value}}{\text{Vesting period in years}}
body.caption: 1,00,000 options at a ₹120 grant-date fair value, vesting over 4 years, gives ₹30 lakh a year.

children.text: So a grant of 1,00,000 options with a fair value of ₹120 each creates a total charge of ₹1.2 crore, recognised as ₹30 lakh a year across the four-year vest. Not one rupee of it leaves the company.

body.text: This is why loss-making Indian tech companies often report a loss that looks worse than their cash position suggests. Analysts frequently look at profit before ESOP cost alongside the reported figure, precisely because the expense is real for accounting and irrelevant for solvency.

children.text: Leavers reduce the cost
When employees leave before vesting, the options are forfeited, and the expense recognised on them is generally reversed. If
10,000 options are forfeited
, the cumulative charge is trued up towards ₹1.08 crore. Attrition, oddly, improves the reported number.

markDefs.definition: Options lost when an employee leaves before vesting, which allows the company to reverse expense already recognised on those options.

body.title: Who applies Ind AS 102, and what goes into the model

children.text: Ind AS 102 applies to listed companies, to unlisted companies above the net worth threshold at which Ind AS becomes mandatory, and to certain NBFCs. Companies outside that net follow the ICAI Guidance Note on Accounting for Share-based Payments instead. Either way, the principle is the same: share-based pay is compensation and must be expensed.

The Black-Scholes inputs your valuer will ask for are the share value on the grant date, the exercise price, the expected life of the option, expected volatility, the risk-free rate and expected dividend yield. For an unlisted company, expected volatility is usually estimated from comparable listed peers, which is why two valuers can produce different numbers for the same grant.

Practical consequence for founders: the grant-date fair value of an option is normally well above its intrinsic value, because it captures the possibility of future gains. Granting options at face value does not make the accounting charge small.

body.title: Compute the Annual Charge
body.prompt: A company grants 1,00,000 options with a grant-date fair value of ₹120 each, vesting evenly over 4 years. What expense does it recognise each year?
body.explanation: 1,00,000 × ₹120 = ₹1.2 crore in total, spread over 4 years, so ₹30 lakh a year. It reduces reported profit without touching cash.

body.title: Does It Cost Cash?
body.question: A startup reports an ESOP expense of ₹4 crore for the year. What has happened to its bank balance as a direct result of that expense?
options: ₹4 crore has been paid out to employees
Nothing. The expense is non-cash, and cash moves only on exercise, buyback or tax payments
₹4 crore has been set aside in a trust
The company owes ₹4 crore to employees at vesting
body.explanation: The charge reflects the value of options granted, recognised over the vesting period. Actual cash movements are separate: money comes in when employees pay the exercise price, and goes out only if the company funds a buyback, a trust or a cash-settled payout.

children.text: Cost Two: Dilution, and What It Does to EPS
Dilution is the cost shareholders feel. Every option that eventually becomes a share reduces everyone else’s percentage, and listed companies must show this through
diluted earnings per share

markDefs.definition: Earnings per share recalculated as if outstanding options and convertibles had become shares. It shows existing shareholders the effect of dilution.

children.text: Take a company earning ₹10 crore with 1,00,00,000 shares outstanding. Basic earnings per share is ₹10. Counting the 1,00,000 options in the share base takes diluted earnings per share to about ₹9.9.

stats.label: Diluted EPS
stats.context: Counting the outstanding options in the share base

stats.label: Effect
stats.context: Small here, but it compounds with every fresh grant and pool top-up

body.title: Dilute the Earnings
body.prompt: A company earns ₹10 crore and has 1,00,00,000 shares outstanding, with 1,00,000 options outstanding as well. Ignoring any exercise proceeds adjustment, what is diluted earnings per share, to two decimal places?
body.explanation: ₹10 crore ÷ 1,01,00,000 shares = about ₹9.9, against ₹10 basic. Real diluted EPS calculations under the accounting standards adjust for assumed exercise proceeds, so treat this as the intuition rather than the full method.

children.text: Cost Three: Cash, When It Finally Moves
Money in.
When employees exercise, they pay the exercise price. At ₹10 on 1,00,000 options, that is ₹10 lakh into the company. Pleasant, but rarely significant.
Money out.
A buyback is the real outflow. Repurchasing 20,000 options at ₹600 costs ₹1.2 crore in cash, which must come from the balance sheet or from investors funding a tender.
Money through.
The company must deduct and deposit TDS on the perquisite at each exercise, and get the timing right. This is an administrative obligation, not a cost, but it is where companies most often slip.
Money abroad.
Where an Indian entity participates in a foreign parent’s plan, there are exchange control and reimbursement arrangements to handle. Specialist advice is not optional here.

columns.label: Accounting cost
points: Arises from the grant, spread over vesting
Based on grant-date fair value, not on any later gain
Reduces reported profit and matters to investors
Reversed for options forfeited by leavers

columns.label: Cash cost
points: Arises only on a buyback or a cash-settled payout
Based on the price actually paid to employees
Hits the cash flow statement and your runway
Entirely within the company’s control, since buybacks are discretionary
The cost employees actually care about

children.text: What This Looks Like at Scale

Paytm is the clearest Indian illustration of how large a non-cash ESOP charge can become. Its disclosed and guided ESOP costs run into four figures in crore terms, and the guided decline shows how a charge unwinds once most grants have vested and fresh grants slow.

body.title: Paytm ESOP cost, reported and guided, ₹ crore

body.label: One-time ESOP acceleration charge, Paytm Q4 FY25
body.context: A non-cash acceleration of ESOP expense recognised in a single quarter, as reported. Accelerated vesting pulls future expense into the present.

children.text: The guided path, around ₹1,174 crore for FY25 falling to roughly ₹558 crore in FY26 and ₹225 crore in FY27, assumes granted options vest and no significant fresh grants are made. That last assumption almost never holds, which is exactly why ESOP cost guidance is worth reading carefully rather than taking at face value.

body.text: Accelerating vesting, whether on an acquisition or as a one-off decision, pulls the remaining expense forward into the current period. It is non-cash, but it can turn a modest reported loss into a large one in a single quarter, and boards should know before they approve it, not after.

body.title: The Board Question
body.scenario: You are the finance lead at a Series C company. The board is reviewing a proposal to top up the ESOP pool by 4% and to extend the post-exit exercise window from 60 days to five years. One director objects that the company "cannot afford more ESOP cost" in a year when it is trying to reach breakeven.
body.prompt: How do you answer, accurately and without overselling?
body.modelAnswer: Separate the three costs. The pool top-up itself creates no expense until options are actually granted, and the charge then arrives as grant-date fair value spread over the vesting period, so the profit and loss impact is gradual and non-cash. It does dilute shareholders, which is a real cost to the people in the room, and that is the honest argument for sizing the top-up from the hiring plan rather than rounding up. The window extension is different again: it creates no additional accounting charge for options already granted and no cash cost at all, though it does mean more vested options survive exits and eventually convert, so dilution is likelier to be realised rather than lapsing back to the pool. On breakeven, the director’s concern is worth addressing directly: if the board is targeting a reported profit figure, the ESOP charge affects it; if it is targeting cash breakeven, the charge is irrelevant and only a future buyback would matter. Ask which of the two the board is actually managing to, because the answer determines whether this proposal is a problem at all.

points: ESOPs carry three separate costs: an accounting expense, dilution, and cash if a buyback ever happens.
Under Ind AS 102 the grant-date fair value is expensed over the vesting period, so 1,00,000 options at a ₹120 fair value cost ₹1.2 crore, or ₹30 lakh a year over four years.
That expense is non-cash. It reduces reported profit without touching the bank balance.
Options forfeited by leavers generally reverse the expense recognised on them.
Dilution shows up for shareholders through diluted EPS, ₹10.00 falling to about ₹9.90 in the example here.
Cash moves in small amounts on exercise and in large amounts on a buyback, which is discretionary.
Accelerating vesting pulls future expense into the current period, as Paytm’s ₹492 crore one-time charge illustrates.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not accounting, tax or investment advice. Company figures are as publicly reported and guidance figures rest on the company’s own stated assumptions. The diluted EPS example is simplified and omits the exercise proceeds adjustment the accounting standards require. Applying Ind AS 102 to a real scheme needs a qualified valuer and auditor.
